claim: Protein acylation is critical for many cellular functions across all domains of life.
source: Protein acylation is critical for many cellular functions across all domains of life.
evidence: This is a general statement about protein acylation supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: In bacteria, lipoproteins have important roles in virulence.
source: In bacteria, lipoproteins have important roles in virulence and are targets for the development of antimicrobials and vaccines.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge and is referenced in the context of the manuscript.

claim: Bacterial lipoproteins are targets for the development of antimicrobials and vaccines.
source: In bacteria, lipoproteins have important roles in virulence and are targets for the development of antimicrobials and vaccines.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dev et al., 1985 in the introduction section.

claim: Bacterial lipoproteins are secreted from the cytosol via the Sec pathway.
source: Bacterial lipoproteins are secreted from the cytosol via the Sec pathway and acylated on an N-terminal cysteine residue through the action of three enzymes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial lipoprotein processing.

claim: Bacterial lipoproteins are acylated on an N-terminal cysteine residue through the action of three enzymes.
source: Bacterial lipoproteins are secreted from the cytosol via the Sec pathway and acylated on an N-terminal cysteine residue through the action of three enzymes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial lipoprotein processing.

claim: In Gram-negative bacteria, the Lol pathway transports lipoproteins to the outer membrane.
source: In Gram-negative bacteria, the Lol pathway transports lipoproteins to the outer membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial lipoprotein trafficking.

claim: The Aat secretion system is a composite system sharing similarity with elements of a type I secretion systems and the Lol pathway.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the Aat secretion system is a composite system sharing similarity with elements of a type I secretion systems and the Lol pathway.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: During secretion, the AatD subunit acylates the substrate CexE on a highly conserved N-terminal glycine residue.
source: During secretion, the AatD subunit acylates the substrate CexE on a highly conserved N-terminal glycine residue.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 8 and mutagenesis experiments in Figure 7.

claim: Mutations disrupting glycine acylation interfere with membrane incorporation and trafficking.
source: Mutations disrupting glycine acylation interfere with membrane incorporation and trafficking.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that G20E mutation prevents acylation and secretion (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: CexE is the first member of a new class of glycine-acylated lipoprotein.
source: Our data reveal CexE as the first member of a new class of glycine-acylated lipoprotein, while Aat represents a new secretion system that displays the substrate lipoprotein on the cell surface.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental data showing glycine acylation.

claim: Aat represents a new secretion system that displays the substrate lipoprotein on the cell surface.
source: Our data reveal CexE as the first member of a new class of glycine-acylated lipoprotein, while Aat represents a new secretion system that displays the substrate lipoprotein on the cell surface.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on the composite nature of the system and its function.

claim: Lipoproteins are key components of bacterial pathogens.
source: As a consequence, lipoproteins are key components of bacterial pathogens and have been targeted for antibiotic and vaccine development (Dev et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dev et al., 1985.

claim: In Gram-negative bacteria, lipoproteins are transported across the inner membrane from the cytosol to the periplasm by the Sec pathway.
source: In Gram-negative bacteria, lipoproteins are transported across the inner membrane from the cytosol to the periplasm by the Sec pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial protein secretion.

claim: In Gram-positive cells, lipoproteins can also be secreted by the TAT pathway.
source: However, in Gram-positive cells, lipoproteins can also be secreted by the TAT pathway (Thompson et al., 2010; Widdick et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Thompson et al., 2010 and Widdick et al., 2011.

claim: The signal peptide inserts into the inner membrane and a diacylglycerol is attached by Lgt to the sulphur moiety of the invariant cysteine at the +1 position of the lipoprotein.
source: The signal peptide inserts into the inner membrane and a diacylglycerol is attached by Lgt to the sulphur moiety of the invariant cysteine at the +1 position of the lipoprotein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial lipoprotein processing.

claim: The signal sequence is cleaved by Lsp (signal peptidase II) exposing the N-terminal amine group of the cysteine for monoacylation by Lnt.
source: The signal sequence is then cleaved by Lsp (signal peptidase II) exposing the N-terminal amine group of the cysteine for monoacylation by Lnt (Gupta et al., 1993; Mizushima, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gupta et al., 1993 and Mizushima, 1984.

claim: The mature triacylated lipoprotein remains embedded in the inner membrane or is localised to the inner leaflet of the outer membrane by the essential Lol pathway.
source: The mature triacylated lipoprotein remains embedded in the inner membrane or is localised to the inner leaflet of the outer membrane by the essential Lol pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial lipoprotein trafficking.

claim: LolCE, in combination with the ATPase LolD, extracts the triacylated lipoprotein from the inner membrane for transport across the periplasm by LolA.
source: LolCE, in combination with the ATPase LolD, extracts the triacylated lipoprotein from the inner membrane for transport across the periplasm by LolA, where it is then incorporated into the inner leaflet of the outer membrane by LolB.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Lol pathway mechanism.

claim: The triacylated lipoprotein is incorporated into the inner leaflet of the outer membrane by LolB.
source: LolCE, in combination with the ATPase LolD, extracts the triacylated lipoprotein from the inner membrane for transport across the periplasm by LolA, where it is then incorporated into the inner leaflet of the outer membrane by LolB.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Lol pathway mechanism.

claim: While the majority of lipoproteins remain periplasmically located, there have been descriptions of surface localised outer membrane lipoproteins.
source: While the majority remain periplasmically located, in recent years, there have been a number of descriptions of surface localised outer membrane lipoproteins (Baldi et al., 2012; Cowles et al., 2011; Konovalova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baldi et al., 2012; Cowles et al., 2011; and Konovalova et al., 2014.

claim: The mechanism of translocation of lipoproteins across the outer membrane to the cell surface remains poorly understood.
source: However, the mechanism of translocation across the outer membrane to the cell surface remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: CexE and Aap are outer membrane proteins associated with enterotoxigenic (ETEC) and enteroaggregative Escherichia coli (EAEC), respectively.
source: Previously, we described two outer membrane proteins (OMPs), CexE and Aap, associated with enterotoxigenic (ETEC) and enteroaggregative Escherichia coli (EAEC), respectively (Crossman et al., 2010; Sheikh et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Crossman et al., 2010 and Sheikh et al., 2002.

claim: CexE has been implicated in prolonged bacterial shedding and increased severity of infection.
source: CexE has been implicated in prolonged bacterial shedding and increased severity of infection (Rivas et al., 2020), whereas Aap influences biofilm formation and gut colonisation (Belmont-Monroy et al., 2020; Sheikh et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rivas et al., 2020.

claim: Aap influences biofilm formation and gut colonisation.
source: CexE has been implicated in prolonged bacterial shedding and increased severity of infection (Rivas et al., 2020), whereas Aap influences biofilm formation and gut colonisation (Belmont-Monroy et al., 2020; Sheikh et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Belmont-Monroy et al., 2020 and Sheikh et al., 2002.

claim: Aap and CexE share only 18% amino acid identity.
source: Despite Aap and CexE sharing only 18% amino acid identity, both proteins are secreted by the Aat system (Belmont-Monroy et al., 2020; Nishi et al., 2003; Rivas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a factual statement about sequence similarity.

claim: Both Aap and CexE are secreted by the Aat system.
source: Despite Aap and CexE sharing only 18% amino acid identity, both proteins are secreted by the Aat system (Belmont-Monroy et al., 2020; Nishi et al., 2003; Rivas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Belmont-Monroy et al., 2020; Nishi et al., 2003; and Rivas et al., 2020.

claim: The Aat system requires five proteins (AatPABCD) to facilitate protein secretion.
source: The Aat system requires five proteins (AatPABCD) to facilitate protein secretion, two of which bear resemblance to components of the type I secretion system (T1SS): an OMP and a periplasmic adaptor protein (PAP).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Aat system components.

claim: Two Aat proteins bear resemblance to components of the type I secretion system (T1SS): an OMP and a periplasmic adaptor protein (PAP).
source: The Aat system requires five proteins (AatPABCD) to facilitate protein secretion, two of which bear resemblance to components of the type I secretion system (T1SS): an OMP and a periplasmic adaptor protein (PAP).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: CexE and Aap substrate molecules are translocated using a two-step mechanism.
source: In contrast to the T1SS, the CexE and Aap substrate molecules are translocated using a two-step mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pilonieta et al., 2007 and other studies.

claim: Aap/CexE is translocated across the inner membrane into the periplasm by the Sec pathway.
source: First, Aap/CexE is translocated across the inner membrane into the periplasm by the Sec pathway (Pilonieta et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pilonieta et al., 2007.

claim: Aap/CexE enters the Aat system to be secreted across the outer membrane.
source: It then enters the Aat system to be secreted across the outer membrane (Belmont-Monroy et al., 2020; Nishi et al., 2003; Rivas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Belmont-Monroy et al., 2020; Nishi et al., 2003; and Rivas et al., 2020.

claim: CexE is post-translationally modified by the Aat system during secretion.
source: While further characterising the two-step secretion mechanism of the Aat system, we noticed that during secretion, CexE is post-translationally modified by the Aat system and this modification is required for the secretion.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 2.

claim: The post-translational modification of CexE is required for secretion.
source: While further characterising the two-step secretion mechanism of the Aat system, we noticed that during secretion, CexE is post-translationally modified by the Aat system and this modification is required for the secretion.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that unmodified CexE is not secreted (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: Following cleavage of the Sec-dependent signal sequence, the N-terminus of CexE is modified by the addition of an acyl chain.
source: Here, we reveal that following cleavage of the Sec-dependent signal sequence, the N-terminus of CexE is modified by the addition of an acyl chain.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 8.

claim: AatD is a homolog of the apolipoprotein N-acyltransferase (Lnt).
source: We demonstrate that AatD is a homolog of the apolipoprotein N-acyltransferase (Lnt).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: AatD is both necessary and sufficient for monoacylation of CexE and Aap.
source: We reveal that AatD is both necessary and sufficient for monoacylation of CexE and Aap.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that AatD alone can acylate CexE in E. coli BL21(DE3) (Figure 5).

claim: CexE lacks an N-terminal cysteine.
source: However, in contrast to Lol lipoprotein substrates, CexE lacks an N-terminal cysteine and instead an invariant glycine is the site of acylation.
evidence: This is supported by N-terminal sequencing data showing GGGNS as the N-terminal sequence.

claim: An invariant glycine is the site of acylation in CexE.
source: However, in contrast to Lol lipoprotein substrates, CexE lacks an N-terminal cysteine and instead an invariant glycine is the site of acylation.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 8 and mutagenesis experiments in Figure 7.

claim: The addition of an N-terminal glycine to the coding sequence of a heterologous protein was sufficient for AatD-catalysed acylation.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that the addition of an N-terminal glycine to the coding sequence of a heterologous protein was sufficient for this novel AatD-catalysed acylation event.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with mCherry fusions shown in Figure 9.

claim: Aap and CexE are members of a novel class of lipoprotein that are secreted through the Aat system.
source: We propose that Aap and CexE are members of a novel class of lipoprotein that are secreted through the Aat system, which is a conglomeration of the Lol pathway and a T1SS.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on the experimental data and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The Aat system is a conglomeration of the Lol pathway and a T1SS.
source: We propose that Aap and CexE are members of a novel class of lipoprotein that are secreted through the Aat system, which is a conglomeration of the Lol pathway and a T1SS.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing homology of Aat components to both Lol and T1SS components (Figure 3).

claim: AatD is a new acyltransferase with glycine as the target of N-palmitoylation.
source: We reveal that AatD is a new acyltransferase with glycine as the target of N-palmitoylation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by mass spectrometry data showing palmitoylation of the N-terminal glycine (Figure 8).

claim: Acylation has a new function in protein secretion.
source: Consequently, we reveal a new function for acylation-protein secretion.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on the finding that acylation is required for CexE secretion.

claim: The Aat system was first identified in EAEC, where it corresponds to the molecular probe (CVD432) used to define this E. coli pathovar.
source: The Aat system was first identified in EAEC, where it corresponds to the molecular probe (CVD432) used to define this E. coli pathovar (Baudry et al., 1990; Nishi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baudry et al., 1990 and Nishi et al., 2003.

claim: The full Aat system and an Aap or CexE homolog was identified in 826 separate nucleotide accessions.
source: The full Aat system and an Aap or CexE homolog was identified in 826 separate nucleotide accessions (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the bioinformatic analysis performed in the study.

claim: The Aat system is distributed more widely than initially anticipated.
source: This revealed that the Aat system is distributed more widely than initially anticipated and is encoded in pathogens with diverse mechanisms of virulence such as ETEC, EAEC, enteropathogenic E. coli, Shiga-toxin producing E. coli, Shigella sp., Salmonella enterica, Citrobacter rodentium, Providencia alcalifaciens, and Yersinia entercolitica (Crossman et al., 2010; Petty et al., 2010; Rivas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the bioinformatic analysis identifying 826 systems and citations to previous studies.

claim: The Aat system is encoded in pathogens with diverse mechanisms of virulence including ETEC, EAEC, enteropathogenic E. coli, Shiga-toxin producing E. coli, Shigella sp., Salmonella enterica, Citrobacter rodentium, Providencia alcalifaciens, and Yersinia entercolitica.
source: This revealed that the Aat system is distributed more widely than initially anticipated and is encoded in pathogens with diverse mechanisms of virulence such as ETEC, EAEC, enteropathogenic E. coli, Shiga-toxin producing E. coli, Shigella sp., Salmonella enterica, Citrobacter rodentium, Providencia alcalifaciens, and Yersinia entercolitica (Crossman et al., 2010; Petty et al., 2010; Rivas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the bioinformatic analysis and citations to Crossman et al., 2010; Petty et al., 2010; and Rivas et al., 2020.

claim: Six separate organisations of the aat operon were identified.
source: From this analysis six separate organisations of the aat operon were identified (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a result from the bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the most common organisation, aap/cexE are separated from the aatPABCD operon by at least 1 kb, accounting for just over half of the aat systems identified.
source: In the most common organisation, aap/cexE are separated from the aatPABCD operon by at least 1 kb. This accounted for just over half of the aat systems identified.
evidence: This is a result from the bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: In just under a quarter of aat operons identified, aap/cexE are within 1 kb of the aatPABCD operon.
source: In just under a quarter of aat operons identified, aap/cexE are within 1 kb of the aatPABCD operon either within 400 bp upstream (18.4%) or 1 kb downstream (4.8%).
evidence: This is a result from the bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: In 25% of the aat systems identified, aatD was separated from aatPABC by >1 kb.
source: In 25% of the aat systems identified, aatD was separated from aatPABC by >1 kb.
evidence: This is a result from the bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Despite differences in operon organization, in every example, the aatPABC genes formed a single operonic unit located with aatD and aap/cexE on a chromosomal pathogenicity island or a large virulence plasmid.
source: However, despite these differences, in every example, the aatPABC genes formed a single operonic unit located with aatD and aap/cexE on a chromosomal pathogenicity island or a large virulence plasmid.
evidence: This is a result from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: AatPABCD have a role in Aap/CexE secretion.
source: These data suggest that AatPABCD have a role in Aap/CexE secretion.
evidence: This is inferred from the genomic organization and supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: A protein with an apparent molecular mass of 11.8 kDa could be detected by western blotting with CexE-specific polyclonal antibodies in culture supernatant fractions collected from ETEC H10407 pCfaD.
source: SDS-PAGE analysis of culture supernatant fractions collected from ETEC H10407 pCfaD revealed a protein with an apparent molecular mass of 11.8 kDa that could be detected by western blotting with CexE-specific polyclonal antibodies (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No protein was detected in the culture supernatant fractions derived from cultures of the ETEC H10407 pCfaD aat or cexE mutants.
source: In contradistinction to the parent strain, no protein was detected in the culture supernatant fractions derived from cultures of the ETEC H10407 pCfaD aat or cexE mutants (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CexE was detected by western blotting with CexE-specific antibodies in whole-cell lysates of ETEC H10407 pCfaD and all aat mutants.
source: CexE was detected by western blotting with CexE-specific antibodies in whole-cell lysates of ETEC H10407 pCfaD and all aat mutants.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CexE could not be detected in the cexE null mutant.
source: In contrast, CexE could not be detected in the cexE null mutant (Figure 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Aat system is essential for CexE secretion.
source: From these data we conclude that the Aat system is essential for CexE secretion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing no secretion in aat mutants (Figure 2A).

claim: CexE appeared as two bands in the parental strain and each of the aat mutants except for aatD when whole-cell lysates were examined by western blotting.
source: Unexpectedly, when the whole-cell lysates of ETEC H10407 pCfaD and its isogenic aat mutants were examined by western blotting, CexE appeared as two bands in the parental strain and each of the aat mutants except for aatD (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The upper band (uCexE) had an apparent molecular mass of 12.7 kDa.
source: The upper band had an apparent molecular mass of 12.7 kDa (uCexE), while the lower band (mCexE) had an apparent molecular mass of 11.8 kDa, which is consistent with the secreted form of CexE recovered from the supernatant fractions.
evidence: This is based on analysis of SDS-PAGE migration shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lower band (mCexE) had an apparent molecular mass of 11.8 kDa, which is consistent with the secreted form of CexE recovered from the supernatant fractions.
source: The upper band had an apparent molecular mass of 12.7 kDa (uCexE), while the lower band (mCexE) had an apparent molecular mass of 11.8 kDa, which is consistent with the secreted form of CexE recovered from the supernatant fractions.
evidence: This is based on analysis of SDS-PAGE migration shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the presence of sodium azide, a protein (preCexE) with an apparent molecular mass of 13.2 kDa was detected.
source: However, in the presence of sodium azide, a protein (preCexE) with an apparent molecular mass of 13.2 kDa was detected (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The difference in molecular mass between uCexE and mCexE was not due to inefficient cleavage of the signal peptide but was due to a post-translational event mediated by AatD.
source: These observations suggest that the difference in molecular mass between uCexE and mCexE was not due to inefficient cleavage of the signal peptide but was due to a post-translational event mediated by AatD.
evidence: This is inferred from the sodium azide experiment (Figure 2C) and the observation that only aatD mutants lack mCexE (Figure 2B).

claim: The deletion of aatD in EAEC 042 resulted in an apparent increase in size of Aap.
source: As noted above for CexE, the deletion of aatD in EAEC 042 resulted in an apparent increase in size of Aap (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The size change of Aap in the aatD mutant could be restored to the wild-type size by complementation with the pJNW plasmid.
source: The size change of Aap in the aatD mutant could be restored to the wild-type size by complementation with the pJNW plasmid.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: AatD can modify Aap and CexE post-translationally.
source: From these data we conclude that AatD can modify Aap and CexE post-translationally and that this modification is required for secretion of the mature substrate molecule to the extracellular milieu.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: The post-translational modification by AatD is required for secretion of the mature substrate molecule to the extracellular milieu.
source: From these data we conclude that AatD can modify Aap and CexE post-translationally and that this modification is required for secretion of the mature substrate molecule to the extracellular milieu.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that unmodified CexE is not secreted (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: AatA is a homolog of the trimeric OMP TolC.
source: In agreement with previous publications, AatA is a homolog of the trimeric OMP TolC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and AatB is a PAP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), components associated with T1SS and drug efflux pumps (Nishi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to Nishi et al., 2003.

claim: AatB is a PAP (periplasmic adaptor protein).
source: In agreement with previous publications, AatA is a homolog of the trimeric OMP TolC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and AatB is a PAP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), components associated with T1SS and drug efflux pumps (Nishi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and citation to Nishi et al., 2003.

claim: AatD was homologous to apolipoprotein N-acyltransferase (Lnt), which is a member of the carbon-nitrogen hydrolase (C-N hydrolase) family (PF00795).
source: In contrast, AatD was not homologous to any T1SS or efflux-associated proteins. Instead, AatD was homologous to apolipoprotein N-acyltransferase (Lnt), which is a member of the carbon-nitrogen hydrolase (C-N hydrolase) family (PF00795) required for bacterial lipoprotein acylation and transport via the Lol system (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Lnt is required for bacterial lipoprotein acylation and transport via the Lol system.
source: In contrast, AatD was not homologous to any T1SS or efflux-associated proteins. Instead, AatD was homologous to apolipoprotein N-acyltransferase (Lnt), which is a member of the carbon-nitrogen hydrolase (C-N hydrolase) family (PF00795) required for bacterial lipoprotein acylation and transport via the Lol system (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Lnt function.

claim: AatD forms a clade with Lnt suggesting that they are functionally related.
source: Comparison of the C-N hydrolase domain of AatD with other members of PF00795 revealed that AatD forms a clade with Lnt suggesting that they are functionally related.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ATPase domain of AatC is part of a clade containing the ATPase domains of LolD.
source: The ATPase domain of AatC is part of a clade containing the ATPase domains of LolD, the ATPase subunit of the LolCDE lipoprotein transporter (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: AatP is more closely related to LolC and LolE than typical ABC transporters of the T1SS, such as HlyB.
source: Similarly, AatP is more closely related to LolC and LolE than typical ABC transporters of the T1SS, such as HlyB (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The homology of AatP, AatC, and AatD to proteins of the Lol pathway suggests that the Aat system is a composite system of a T1SS and the Lol lipoprotein trafficking system.
source: The homology of AatP, AatC, and AatD to proteins of the Lol pathway suggests that the Aat system is a composite system of a T1SS and the Lol lipoprotein trafficking system.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the presence of AatD and 17-ODYA, CexE was fluorescently labelled.
source: In the presence of AatD and 17-ODYA, CexE was fluorescently labelled; in the absence of either 17-ODYA or AatD, no fluorescence was observed.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the absence of either 17-ODYA or AatD, no fluorescence was observed on CexE.
source: In the presence of AatD and 17-ODYA, CexE was fluorescently labelled; in the absence of either 17-ODYA or AatD, no fluorescence was observed.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Only mCexE was labelled indicating that uCexE is an unacylated form of CexE.
source: Moreover, only mCexE was labelled indicating that uCexE is an unacylated form of CexE; counterintuitively, the acylated form (mCexE) migrates faster on SDS-PAGE than the unacylated uCexE.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The acylated form (mCexE) migrates faster on SDS-PAGE than the unacylated uCexE.
source: Moreover, only mCexE was labelled indicating that uCexE is an unacylated form of CexE; counterintuitively, the acylated form (mCexE) migrates faster on SDS-PAGE than the unacylated uCexE.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Only the acylated versions of Aap and CexE were present in the culture supernatant.
source: Furthermore, only the acylated versions of Aap and CexE were present in the culture supernatant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only mCexE was detectable by western blotting in the membrane fraction of the parent strain and the aatPABC mutants.
source: After separation by SDS-PAGE, only mCexE was detectable by western blotting in the membrane fraction of the parent strain and the aatPABC mutants; no mCexE could be detected in the membranes recovered from the aatD mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: No mCexE could be detected in the membranes recovered from the aatD mutant.
source: After separation by SDS-PAGE, only mCexE was detectable by western blotting in the membrane fraction of the parent strain and the aatPABC mutants; no mCexE could be detected in the membranes recovered from the aatD mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both mCexE and uCexE could be detected in whole-cell lysates of ETEC H10407 pCfaD.
source: In contrast, both mCexE and uCexE could be detected in whole-cell lysates of ETEC H10407 pCfaD and only uCexE could be detected in whole-cell lysates of the aatD mutant.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only uCexE could be detected in whole-cell lysates of the aatD mutant.
source: In contrast, both mCexE and uCexE could be detected in whole-cell lysates of ETEC H10407 pCfaD and only uCexE could be detected in whole-cell lysates of the aatD mutant.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: AatD is an acyltransferase that mediates post-translational modification of CexE by the addition of one or more acyl chains.
source: These data suggest that AatD is an acyltransferase that mediates post-translational modification of CexE by the addition of one or more acyl chains.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the 17-ODYA labeling experiments (Figure 4).

claim: When CexE and AatD were produced together in E. coli BL21, mCexE migrated further on SDS-PAGE.
source: However, when CexE and AatD were produced together, mCexE migrated further (Figure 5).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: AatD was necessary for the modification of CexE.
source: These data suggest AatD was necessary for the modification of CexE.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experiment in E. coli BL21 (Figure 5).

claim: The C-N hydrolase family of proteins have a known conserved catalytic triad.
source: The C-N hydrolase family of proteins have a known conserved catalytic triad, which in the case of Lnt is E267, K335, and C387.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the C-N hydrolase family.

claim: In Lnt, the catalytic triad consists of E267, K335, and C387.
